I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :) - 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC... - Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid. - The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc. - 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map. - Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry - Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode. It's deployed here: https://karpathy.ai/usaciv/ and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer: Media

Banger paper from NVIDIA on context management for agents. (bookmark it) They suggest a co-design where models are trained to manage their own context, and inference engines are built to serve it efficiently at scale. Context management is an important primitive for long-running agents. Today, the harness usually decides when to compact, by summarizing the history once the window fills. The NVIDIA team gave models a context API inside NOOA, their open-source agent harness, so the model decides when and what to compact. They compared both approaches on document research and ML engineering tasks at budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. At a 32K budget, GPT 6.1 went from 21% to 56% on OfficeQA Pro v2 when it managed its own context. Kimi improved accuracy with up to 41% fewer input tokens. Models differ a lot in how often they call the API and how early they compact, and small prompt changes shift that timing. Inference engines can make these edits cheaper too. Reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit cut prefill compute by up to 15% per request with no measurable accuracy change. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34147 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/letting-models-manage-their-own-context-where-we-stand-2611.34147

Highly recommended read. It's a really neat idea that could help scale multi-agent swarms. The proposed technique, called speculative encoding, lets supported models reuse computation already spent processing the same context. This could reduce delay when several agents need that context or when a task moves between models. For example, imagine several agents reviewing a very long contract. One model processes it first; speculative encoding translates its internal representations into an approximate cache another model can use to answer questions about termination clauses. This could also complement model routing, where different tasks go to stronger or cheaper models. Switching models usually means processing the shared context, because their internal caches aren't directly interchangeable. With long documents and frequent handoffs, that repeated prefill can become a bottleneck. There's a lot more to figure out here. How much speed does this save across a complete agent workflow? How does translation affect answer quality over repeated handoffs? And when does the translation cost outweigh the savings? I think it's a very promising research direction. Multi-agent swarms shouldn't have to read context more than once. Introducing speculative encoding, one 2.35B MoE that directly translates between any model's hidden states. Across 7 models, it keeps 96.9% of base accuracy and cuts prefill latency by up to 7.5× on long documents…
